title: Risk Assessment: Independent implement phases (slice-scoped DAG + stacked PRs)
summary: Issue #2137 splits the monolithic implement phase into a DAG of independent slices, each with its own branch, fresh agent team, BRC consensus round, and stacked PR. The change is large (~1,500-2,500 LOC across orchestrator, gateway, plan_parser, models, dependency_graph) and touches the most security-sensitive code paths in the pipeline (BRC tracker namespacing, gateway push allowlists, pipeline_id keying everywhere). Refine-phase HITL has narrowed many design questions, but residual technical risk remains HIGH in three clusters: (1) pipeline_id hierarchy fan-out across every consumer of the message bus (audit, heartbeat, overseer, MCP tools, gateway authorization); (2) stacked-PR rebase reconciliation under partial failure (sibling slices keep running, mid-stack PR closures block descendants, GitHub auto-retarget edge cases on squash merges); (3) plan-ingestion forest validation as the single enforcement point with no runtime backstop. Token cost is a NEW operational risk because the design uses unbounded slice parallelism + identical full reviewer roster per slice, multiplying implement-phase cost by slice count.
recommendation_rationale: The design is sound and the refine-phase HITL has resolved the major architectural choices coherently, but the surface area touched (every consumer of pipeline_id, the gateway push-authorization layer, the plan-ingestion validator, the orchestrator scheduler, branch/PR creation, and the deadlock/HITL escalation paths) is unusually wide. The implement phase MUST land all changes in a single PR per the issue's own framing, and the rollout has no feature flag, so a regression in any one of the touched subsystems will block the entire pipeline. Mitigations focus on (a) making pipeline_id hierarchy a typed first-class concept rather than a string-prefix convention, (b) keeping the forest validator deterministic and unit-tested independently of the planner LLM, (c) bounding slice concurrency conservatively on first roll-out despite the refine decision to leave it unbounded, and (d) monitoring rebase-reconciler error rates to catch GitHub auto-retarget gaps.

risks.title: pipeline_id hierarchy must be threaded through every BRC / message bus consumer
risks.impact: Slice-scoped CONSENSUS_PROPOSE / CONSENSUS_ACK messages misrouted, peer_consensus tracker collisions, audit log keying drift, OVERSEER_ALERT visibility loss; in worst case a slice's BRC stalls silently because reviewers see messages under the parent pipeline_id while producers send under the slice ID (or vice-versa).
risks.description: Decision-14 selected the hybrid namespacing: cross-slice messages (HEARTBEAT, OVERSEER_ALERT) keep flat pipeline_id; BRC consensus messages (CONSENSUS_*) use nested `issue-N/slice-M`. The current code (orchestrator/peer_consensus.py:69-180; orchestrator/routes/pipelines.py state lookups; gateway message-store routes; mcp__brc__*, mcp__progress__*, mcp__sdlc__* tools; audit log filenames in `.egg-state/brc-history/<id>-<phase>.json`) all key on a single `pipeline_id` string. Every lookup path that consumes `pipeline_id` from a message MUST be classified as 'BRC-scoped' (slice-aware) or 'cross-slice-scoped' (flat). A miss in either direction silently breaks routing — producers will time out waiting for ACKs that landed under a different key, and reviewers will never see the proposal.
affected_files: shared/egg_agent/mcp tools (brc, progress, sdlc, task, phase namespaces)

mitigation.strategy: Introduce a typed `PipelineRef` value object (pipeline_id + optional slice_id) at the boundary between the orchestrator and message bus. Refactor lookup paths to take `PipelineRef` rather than `str`, with explicit `.flat()` / `.brc_scoped()` accessors. Add a unit-test matrix that enumerates each MCP tool / BRC endpoint and asserts which scope it uses; CI must fail when a new lookup site is added without classification. Keep an end-to-end integration test that runs a 3-slice pipeline and verifies CONSENSUS_PROPOSE / CONSENSUS_ACK flow is correctly isolated per slice while HEARTBEAT / OVERSEER_ALERT are visible pipeline-wide.
mitigation.residual_risk: MEDIUM — typing eliminates the silent mis-routing class, but every existing lookup site is an audit point and the integration test must cover edge cases (re-review, re-confirmation, NACK aggregation #2142, stale-version rejections)

risks.review_reason: Pipeline_id is the consensus tracker primary key; getting the hierarchy wrong corrupts the BRC protocol invariants documented in #2142 (NACK aggregation) and #1925 (event-driven wait semantics).

risks.title: Stacked-PR rebase reconciler relies on GitHub's auto-retarget; squash-merge and mid-stack closure edge cases
risks.impact: Child slice PRs become unmergeable when parent PR is squash-merged (commit identity loss), parent PR is closed without merging (decision-2 says siblings keep running), or rebase conflicts cascade upward through the stack. In the worst case, a 5-slice stack requires manual intervention on every child after the root slice merges.
risks.description: Decision-16 chose hybrid (GitHub auto-retarget primary + periodic reconciler fallback). External research (GitHub's native stacked PRs guidance, github.github.com/gh-stack/, community.github.com #17880, #176698) confirms: (a) auto-retarget fires reliably only when parent merges via GitHub UI / `gh pr merge`; force-push or branch deletion breaks the chain; (b) squash-merges trigger artificial conflicts because original commits disappear from history — only `git rebase --onto` resolves these cleanly; (c) mid-stack PR closure blocks all descendants until the stack is unstacked and re-created; (d) cascading rebase conflicts can require manual resolution on every PR above the conflict point. The reconciler must handle all four cases and the orchestrator must distinguish 'auto-retarget already happened' from 'auto-retarget never fired and we need to act'. Decision-2 (siblings continue on slice failure) compounds this: a failed slice may keep its PR open in 'closed/abandoned' state, leaving descendants in limbo.
affected_files: gateway routes for PR creation (gh pr create wrappers)

mitigation.strategy: (1) Use `git rebase --onto` (not plain `git rebase`) for all reconciler operations to handle squash-merge correctly. (2) Detect parent PR state before rebasing: distinguish 'merged via UI' (auto-retarget already happened, skip), 'merged via squash' (must rebase --onto), 'closed without merge' (escalate to HITL — descendants are stuck), 'force-pushed' (must rebase). (3) Emit OVERSEER_ALERT when reconciler finds >N retries on the same child PR (likely a real merge conflict requiring human resolution). (4) Reconciler must be idempotent — running it twice on the same state is a no-op; this lets it run on a periodic timer without coordination locks. (5) Document the manual recovery procedure for the failed-parent case in docs/guides/sdlc-pipeline.md before merging #2137.
mitigation.residual_risk: MEDIUM — even with `git rebase --onto`, cascading conflicts on a 5+ deep stack will routinely require human resolution; the reconciler can detect but not resolve

risks.review_reason: Stacked-PR mechanics are GitHub-API surface and prone to subtle UX regressions. Manual review of reconciler edge cases by an engineer familiar with `gh stack` / Graphite-style workflows is needed.

risks.title: Forest validation only at plan ingestion — no runtime backstop
risks.impact: If a malformed contract (multi-parent slices, dependency cycles, references to non-existent slices) reaches the orchestrator scheduler, it will either hang waiting for impossible parent completions or crash with an unhelpful KeyError mid-pipeline.
risks.description: Decision-18 selected enforcement at `_populate_contract_from_plan` only (not at the reviewer prompt, not at runtime). This makes the validator the SINGLE point of failure for contract well-formedness. Two failure modes: (a) a future code change to the contract loader bypasses the validator (e.g., a migration path that loads a legacy contract directly into the orchestrator); (b) a contract is mutated post-ingestion (e.g., HITL adds a slice via add-decision) and the new shape isn't re-validated. Neither is hypothetical — the codebase already has multiple contract-loading paths (orchestrator/routes/pipelines.py:10860+, plus checkpoint restoration, plus the upcoming migration shim from decision-7).

mitigation.strategy: (1) Make the validator a pure function on the Slice list, not coupled to the loader, and call it from EVERY contract-load path: ingestion, checkpoint restore, migration shim, and the orchestrator scheduler entry. (2) Add a startup invariant in the slice scheduler that re-runs validation when it loads `contract.slices[]`; on violation, fail fast with a structured error and OVERSEER_ALERT. (3) Cover the validator with property-based tests (hypothesis or similar) that generate random DAGs and assert: well-formed forest accepts; multi-parent rejected; cycles rejected; dangling deps rejected. (4) Add a regression test for the migration shim from decision-7 that loads pre-#2137 contracts (with `phases[]` in legacy multi-parent form, if any exist) and verifies validation either translates them or rejects them clearly.
mitigation.residual_risk: LOW — defense-in-depth at all load paths catches the silent-corruption class; remaining risk is logical bugs in the validator itself, mitigated by property tests

risks.title: Token cost blow-up: N slices × full reviewer roster × unbounded parallelism
risks.impact: A 10-slice ticket runs 10× the implement-phase token spend of today's monolithic flow because decision-12 mandates identical full roster per slice (coder + tester + documenter + reviewer_code + reviewer_code_holistic + reviewer_contract + reviewer_security + reviewer_concurrency = 8 roles × N slices) and decision-5 leaves slice concurrency unbounded. Worst-case 15-slice ticket from feedback Q1 = 120 agent-instances launched simultaneously. Anthropic rate-limit throttling, gateway 429s, and GHA queue saturation are all plausible at this fan-out.
risks.description: Today's implement phase is single-pass with one shared agent team. The proposed model multiplies cost by slice count without sharing reviewer context across slices. While the token-savings goal of #2137 is to AVOID compaction (which improves quality at fixed cost), the cost shape inverts: a previously-oversized ticket that runs in compacted mode at cost C will now run uncompacted at cost ~Nx where N is the slice count (typical 3-7 per refine feedback, worst 10-15). Without a concurrency cap, 15 slices × 8 roles each = 120 simultaneous agent containers. The gateway, orchestrator HTTP layer, and Anthropic API rate limits are not designed for this concurrency.

mitigation.strategy: (1) Despite decision-5 being 'unbounded', ship with `max_parallel_slices` defaulting to 5 (the value the refiner suggested in feedback Q1) as an OPERATIONAL safety limit, separate from the design choice. The orchestrator should still be capable of unbounded parallelism architecturally — the cap is a runtime config. (2) Emit a warning at plan ingestion when the resulting DAG has a wave wider than the cap, telling the operator how to raise the cap. (3) Add a per-slice token-spend metric to the audit log so operators can size the cap empirically. (4) Document the cost shape (10-slice ticket ≈ 10× implement-phase cost) prominently in the rollout note so operators understand the trade-off. (5) Ensure single-slice pipelines (the common case for small tickets) skip slice scheduling overhead entirely — fall back to today's monolithic implement flow when len(slices) == 1.
mitigation.residual_risk: MEDIUM — the cost multiplier is intrinsic to the design; mitigation caps blast radius but doesn't eliminate the inversion vs. compaction. Operator guidance and per-slice cost visibility are the long-term controls.

risks.review_reason: Cost inversion changes the operational economics of large tickets. The product owner should be aware that #2137's win is quality (no compaction), not cost — the cost goes UP, not down.

risks.title: Gateway push-authorization layer must understand slice branches
risks.impact: A malformed slice-branch allowlist could (a) reject legitimate pushes from a slice's coder agent (hard fail, slice can't make progress); (b) accept pushes from one slice's agent to another slice's branch (cross-slice contamination, BRC integrity violation). Worst case: a coder in slice-2 pushes code that lands on slice-1's branch and is reviewed by slice-1's reviewers under the wrong context.
risks.description: Today's gateway agent_restrictions.py keys push allowlists on (pipeline_id, role) → branch_pattern. Slice branches `egg/issue-N/slice-M` introduce a new dimension. Each slice has its own coder/tester/etc. agent identities, and the gateway must verify that 'agent X spawned for slice-3' can ONLY push to `egg/issue-N/slice-3` and not to `egg/issue-N/slice-1`. Cross-slice push authorization is the primary security boundary protecting BRC integrity.
affected_files: orchestrator/concurrent_executor.py (agent spawn — must pass slice_id to gateway as part of identity)

mitigation.strategy: (1) Extend agent identity (the credential/role tuple the gateway sees) to include `slice_id`; the gateway constructs the expected branch pattern from `(pipeline_id, slice_id, role)` and rejects any push that doesn't match. (2) Add a gateway-level integration test that spawns two slices, attempts a cross-slice push, and asserts the gateway returns 403. (3) Audit-log every push with the resolved (pipeline_id, slice_id, role, branch) tuple so cross-slice contamination is detectable post-hoc. (4) Coordinate with the file-boundary system (today's per-role file allowlist) — slice branches inherit the producer-role boundaries; reviewer roles still cannot push code regardless of slice.
mitigation.residual_risk: LOW — gateway authorization is the well-trodden path in this codebase; adding slice_id to the identity tuple is mechanical; integration test catches the silent-cross-slice-push class

risks.review_reason: Push authorization is the security boundary between agents. A regression here breaks BRC integrity. Reviewer should be familiar with the gateway's existing per-role allowlist model.

risks.title: Hybrid deadlock detection (60s grace + DAG walk) — race window and HITL escalation latency
risks.impact: Within the 60s grace window, downstream slices that depend on a failed slice keep running and burning tokens. If the grace window is mis-tuned (too short → premature abort of recoverable failures; too long → wasted spend on doomed work), operator experience degrades.
risks.description: Decision-10 chose hybrid: 60s grace period after a slice failure for HITL resolution; if not resolved, walk the DAG and abort downstream. Two race windows: (a) [t=0, t=60s]: slice-A failed, downstream slice-B is running; if HITL doesn't resolve by t=60s, slice-B is aborted mid-execution (token waste; partial state in slice-B's branch may need cleanup). (b) [t=60s+]: DAG walk runs; if slice-B has already started, must distinguish 'kill in flight' vs. 'mark blocked for new spawns'. Decision-2 says siblings keep running, but downstream slices that depend on the failed slice are explicitly blocked — this is the case the DAG walk handles.

mitigation.strategy: (1) Implement the DAG walk as a pure function over the slice graph + status map; unit-test it on known-bad shapes. (2) The 60s grace timer starts when the slice is OFFICIALLY marked failed (HITL escalation triggered, max_cycles tripped, or agent crash detected — all three paths must converge to the same timer-start event). (3) When grace expires, downstream slice teardown must be idempotent: if the agent team has already exited cleanly, no-op; if mid-execution, send SIGTERM with a 30s drain window before SIGKILL. (4) Audit-log the entire failure cascade (failed slice → grace timer → HITL response or DAG walk → downstream abort list) so the failure trace is reconstructable. (5) Make the 60s grace configurable via a contract setting so operators can tune per-pipeline.
mitigation.residual_risk: LOW — the design is well-bounded; teardown idempotency and audit logging cover the operational concerns

risks.title: Two-tier max_cycles (slice=3, pipeline=10) — global cap can starve later slices
risks.impact: If slice-1 burns 5 cycles before ACKing and slice-2 burns 5 more, the global pipeline cap (10) is exhausted before slice-3 can even start. Slice-3 escalates HITL on first NACK because the global budget is gone, even though its local cycle count is 0.
risks.description: Decision-9 picked two-tier (local cap 3, global cap 10). Math: with 5+ slices, the global cap can be exhausted by 'noisy' early slices, leaving later slices with zero budget. This is a confusing operator experience because 'slice-3 escalated HITL after 1 NACK' looks like a slice-3 problem when it's actually a budget-exhaustion problem. Today's per-phase cycle accounting (orchestrator's `max_cycles` setting) is per-phase and doesn't aggregate across phases.

mitigation.strategy: (1) When the global cap trips, emit a SPECIFIC OVERSEER_ALERT identifying the cause as 'global budget exhausted' rather than 'slice X failed' so operators understand the root cause. (2) Audit-log per-slice cycle consumption so the operator can spot the budget-hog slice retroactively. (3) Document the math: 'global cap = 10 means roughly 3 noisy slices or 10 modestly-noisy slices'. (4) Consider raising the global default to 15 if early dogfooding shows starvation (the 10 default came from refine-phase HITL but isn't load-tested). (5) Make global cap configurable per-pipeline so large tickets can opt-in to a higher budget.
mitigation.residual_risk: LOW — even with starvation, the failure mode is HITL escalation (visible, recoverable), not silent corruption

risks.title: Phase → Slice migration shim for in-flight pipelines and external consumers
risks.impact: Pipelines started pre-#2137 with `contract.phases[]` continue running under the new orchestrator. If the migration shim has bugs (missed field, dependency translation glitches, JSON schema drift), in-flight pipelines crash mid-execution.
risks.description: Decision-7 chose 'rename + one-version migration shim that auto-translates phases[] → slices[] on contract load'. The shim must handle: (a) contracts loaded by orchestrator on startup (pipeline restoration); (b) contracts loaded by checkpoint replay; (c) contracts loaded by MCP tools (mcp__sdlc__show_contract — does it return slices or phases? must remain backward-compatible for one version); (d) contracts loaded by the GHA action / babysit_pr (out of scope per refine-phase decision-8 but the same code may load contracts). External consumers reading the contract JSON directly (e.g., custom tooling, dashboards, the upcoming #2199 MCP slice control) must understand both shapes during the transition.

mitigation.strategy: (1) Migration shim runs at the lowest contract-load layer (model __init__ or a single classmethod) so EVERY load path picks it up automatically — no per-call-site translation. (2) Shim is one-direction: phases[] → slices[]; never write phases[] back. (3) Schema-version field on the contract (`schemaVersion`) is bumped from '1.0' to '1.1' on first slice-aware write; loaders treat 1.0 as needing translation, 1.1 as native. (4) MCP tools return the new shape (`slices[]`) but accept reads that include either field name during transition. (5) Add a one-version deprecation notice in the docs that the legacy `phases[]` field will be removed in the next minor release. (6) Property-test the shim on randomly-generated 1.0 contracts to verify lossless round-trip.
mitigation.residual_risk: LOW — migration shims are well-understood; the schemaVersion bump is the standard control

risks.title: Lens reviewers (security, concurrency) are PER-SLICE only — cross-slice regressions invisible
risks.impact: A security regression that spans two slices (e.g., slice-1 introduces a token-bearing config, slice-2 logs that config in a debug print) is caught by neither slice's reviewer_security because each only sees its own diff. Same for concurrency — a deadlock pattern split across slices is invisible to per-slice reviewer_concurrency.
risks.description: Decision-13 (correcting decision-3) selected per-slice lens-reviewer scope, ADVISORY (not CRITICAL — promotion deferred to #1997). Cross-slice regressions are an inherent blind spot of per-slice review. The MITIGATION is reviewer_code_holistic running once on the merged pipeline branch (per #2126's motivation), but reviewer_security and reviewer_concurrency don't get the same cross-slice pass. This is an explicit trade-off the refine phase made for cost reasons, but it's a real residual risk.
affected_files: Documentation: docs/architecture/reviewer-roster.md (must call out the per-slice limitation)

mitigation.strategy: (1) Document the limitation explicitly in the rollout note so security-conscious operators know to manually review the merged stack before approving. (2) Add a follow-up issue (similar to how #2199 was filed for MCP control) tracking the cross-slice lens pass — likely deferred to post-#1997 when lenses are CRITICAL and the cost calculation changes. (3) For HIGH-RISK pipelines (operator-tagged), consider running reviewer_security once at PR-phase entry on the diff-of-diffs as an opt-in safeguard.
mitigation.residual_risk: MEDIUM — the gap is real and the mitigation is documentation + opt-in. A future security incident traceable to a cross-slice regression is plausible but contained (lens reviewers are advisory today, not the primary security control).

risks.review_reason: Per-slice security-lens scope is a deliberate cost trade-off. Confirm the product owner is comfortable with the documented limitation.

risks.title: Auto-serialization heuristic gives planner full control over slice ordering
risks.impact: If the planner (LLM) emits a `serialized_chain_order` that minimizes its prompt-perceived merge friction but actually MAXIMIZES real merge friction, the resulting stack has more rebase conflicts than necessary. Recovery requires HITL re-planning.
risks.description: Decision-17 chose 'planner emits explicit serialized_chain_order; heuristic is fallback'. The planner's judgment on file-overlap and fan-out is unverified — it's an LLM, not a static analyzer. A well-meaning planner might serialize slices in an order that's logically reasonable but file-physically conflict-heavy. The fallback heuristic (cluster by `files_affected` Jaccard, order by descending fan-out) is ALSO unverified at scale — Jaccard overlap is a proxy for merge-friction, not a guarantee.

mitigation.strategy: (1) Reviewer_plan must spot-check serialized_chain_order during plan review — explicitly call this out in the reviewer's prompt template. (2) Add a static check: if any two adjacent slices in the serialized chain have >50% file overlap, emit a plan-phase warning (advisory, not NACK). (3) Log the chosen ordering in the audit trail so post-mortem analysis can compare 'planner picked' vs. 'heuristic picked' outcomes. (4) Document the operator escape hatch: HITL approver can override the order during plan approval (refine-phase decision-17 says 'no separate HITL prompt for the choice itself' but the operator can NACK the plan and request a re-plan).
mitigation.residual_risk: LOW — worst case is extra rebase work, not pipeline failure; the audit trail enables empirical tuning

risks.title: Slice-addressable internal hooks must exist even though MCP verbs (#2199) are out of scope
risks.impact: If #2137 ships without slice-addressable internal APIs, #2199 (per-slice MCP control) becomes a much larger refactor. Operators are stuck with phase-granularity controls (`restart_phase`, `restart_agent`) that disrupt sibling slices when only one needs intervention.
risks.description: Refine feedback Q4 explicitly states: '#2137 should expose the internal slice-addressable hooks; the MCP verb layer itself is out of scope for #2137 and lands in #2199'. This is an architectural pre-requirement for #2199 that #2137 must satisfy without itself shipping the verbs. The slice scheduler must already know how to teardown / respawn / query a slice in isolation — these capabilities must be reachable as Python functions even if no MCP verb exposes them yet.

mitigation.strategy: (1) Define the internal API surface explicitly: `restart_slice(pipeline_id, slice_id)`, `respawn_slice_agent(pipeline_id, slice_id, role)`, `get_slice_status(pipeline_id, slice_id)`, `list_slices(pipeline_id)`. These live as Python functions in the orchestrator, callable but not yet wired to MCP. (2) Unit-test each function independently of the MCP layer. (3) #2199 then ONLY adds the MCP wiring, not the underlying logic. (4) Document the API surface in docs/architecture/orchestrator-internal-api.md so #2199's planner can plan against a known shape.
mitigation.residual_risk: LOW — explicit API definition + unit tests catch the 'forgot to expose' class; the cost is moving some abstraction work from #2199 to #2137

risks.title: Worktree lifecycle: per-slice worktrees must be cleaned up on slice failure / abort
risks.impact: Orphaned worktrees accumulate on disk if a slice is aborted mid-execution and its worktree isn't torn down. Long-running orchestrator hosts run out of disk; new pipelines fail to start.
risks.description: Today's `create_phase_worktree` is per-pipeline. Per-slice worktrees multiply the count by slice fan-out. If the deadlock detector (R6) aborts downstream slices, their worktrees must be removed. The current code path for worktree cleanup may not handle the 'aborted before agent team finished' case cleanly — there are issues like #2155 (re-verify on PipelineNotFoundError instead of nuking worktrees) that show this is a delicate area.

mitigation.strategy: (1) Per-slice worktrees use a deterministic path scheme: `/home/egg/.egg-worktrees/<pipeline_id>/<slice_id>/<role>`. (2) On slice abort, sweep the entire `<pipeline_id>/<slice_id>/` subtree atomically. (3) On orchestrator startup, scan the worktree root and reconcile against active pipelines/slices — orphans are cleaned up. (4) Audit-log every worktree creation and removal so disk usage is traceable. (5) Add a periodic disk-usage metric to the orchestrator's health endpoint.
mitigation.residual_risk: LOW — the pattern is well-established in #2155 / #2186 (per-repo worktree creation errors); slice fan-out just multiplies the subject count

risks.title: Plan-phase prompt update: planner LLM must learn to emit slices[] with serialized_chain_order
risks.impact: The planner is an LLM. If its prompt template doesn't clearly articulate the new schema (slices[] vs phases[], dependencies as forest with ≤1 parent, optional serialized_chain_order field), it will emit malformed plans that the validator rejects. Each rejection round burns plan-phase BRC cycles and operator time.
risks.description: The plan parser today handles a YAML/markdown fence with a known schema. #2137 changes that schema (rename, add serialized_chain_order, enforce forest constraint). The planner LLM's prompt MUST be updated to match, with examples and explicit constraints. Without this, the planner happily emits the OLD schema and the new validator rejects it on every attempt — infinite NACK loop until the global cycle cap trips.

mitigation.strategy: (1) Update the plan-phase system prompt with the new schema, including a worked example of a 3-slice forest with one chain serialization. (2) Update the plan-phase reviewer prompt to NACK plans missing `slices[]` or with multi-parent slices. (3) Add a fast-fail path in the parser: when the parser detects `phases[]` from a planner that should be emitting `slices[]`, return a structured error WITH the corrected schema embedded so the next round of the planner LLM has the example in context. (4) Manually verify on 3 representative tickets (small, medium, oversized) that the planner emits valid slices on first try.
mitigation.residual_risk: LOW — LLM prompt iteration is a well-trodden path; worst case is a couple of plan-phase BRC rounds until the prompt converges

risks.title: Single-slice (small ticket) fallback path must skip slice scheduling overhead
risks.impact: Small tickets that fit in one slice should NOT pay the slice-scheduling overhead (extra branch creation, extra BRC tracker, extra PR base-branch resolution). If they do, every small ticket gets slower with no quality benefit.
risks.description: Most tickets are small (single phase today). Slice scheduling overhead must amortize to zero on len(slices) == 1. This isn't called out in the issue but is an obvious operational concern: the win for #2137 is on LARGE tickets (the 33K LOC / 41 file regression benchmark from #2105); small tickets should be unchanged.
affected_files: orchestrator/run_loop (scheduler entry — fast-path for single slice)

mitigation.strategy: (1) Detect len(slices) == 1 at scheduler entry; route to today's monolithic implement-phase code with `egg/issue-N` branch (no `/slice-1` suffix) and flat pipeline_id for BRC. (2) Single-slice contracts emit `slices: [{id: slice-1, ...}]` in the contract for schema consistency, but the orchestrator treats them specially. (3) Add an integration test for single-slice (today's common case) and assert no behavioral change vs. pre-#2137. (4) Branch naming for single-slice: `egg/issue-N` (unchanged), not `egg/issue-N/slice-1` — preserves PR URL backward compatibility.
mitigation.residual_risk: LOW — fast-path is a localized optimization; integration test catches the regression

risks.title: babysit_pr left out of scope — ensure slice machinery doesn't accidentally couple to it
risks.impact: If #2137's slice infrastructure accidentally creates new coupling to babysit_pr's branch/role conventions, #2063 (the babysit_pr-related work) becomes harder.
risks.description: Refine-phase decision-8 carved out babysit_pr as a follow-up (#2199-style). The slice machinery in #2137 should be designed so it does NOT accidentally depend on babysit_pr's `egg/babysit-pr/{pr}/{sha}/{role}` branch convention. Branch-pattern resolution must remain orthogonal between SDLC pipelines (issue-N) and babysit_pr (PR-N).

mitigation.strategy: (1) Branch-pattern resolution takes a typed `PipelineMode` enum (ISSUE / BABYSIT / CUSTOM) as input and returns a typed `BranchPattern` value object — no string concatenation at the use site. (2) Add a unit test asserting that ISSUE mode produces `egg/issue-N/slice-M` and BABYSIT mode produces `egg/babysit-pr/{pr}/{sha}/{role}` and they never collide. (3) Document the carve-out in code comments at the branch-resolution function so future maintainers understand the orthogonality.
mitigation.residual_risk: NEGLIGIBLE — typed enums prevent accidental coupling

areas_requiring_human_review.area: R1: pipeline_id hierarchy threading through every BRC consumer
areas_requiring_human_review.reason: Pipeline_id is the BRC primary key; getting hierarchy wrong corrupts the consensus protocol invariants from #2142 (NACK aggregation), #1925 (event-driven wait), and #1998 (conditional ACK). The audit must enumerate every lookup site and classify it.
areas_requiring_human_review.suggested_reviewer: Engineer familiar with peer_consensus.py and the BRC message-store layer

areas_requiring_human_review.area: R2: stacked-PR rebase reconciler edge cases
areas_requiring_human_review.reason: GitHub auto-retarget has documented gaps on squash-merges, force-pushes, mid-stack closures, and force-deletes. The reconciler must use `git rebase --onto` and detect parent PR state correctly. Reviewer should be familiar with `gh stack`, Graphite, or similar stacked-PR tooling.

areas_requiring_human_review.area: R4: token cost inversion on large tickets
areas_requiring_human_review.reason: #2137's win is quality (avoiding compaction), not cost. Large tickets cost MORE under the new model (Nx implement-phase cost where N = slice count, up to 15 worst-case from feedback Q1). Product owner should confirm comfort with this trade-off and the `max_parallel_slices` operational cap.

Push authorization is the security boundary between agents. Cross-slice contamination would silently break BRC integrity. Reviewer should be familiar with gateway/agent_restrictions.py and the per-role allowlist model.

areas_requiring_human_review.area: R9: per-slice lens-reviewer scope as a security trade-off
areas_requiring_human_review.reason: Decision-13 deliberately accepted that cross-slice security regressions are invisible to per-slice reviewer_security. This is a documented limitation; product owner should sign off that the documented mitigation (manual stack review for HIGH-RISK pipelines) is sufficient until #1997 promotes lenses to CRITICAL.

rollback_plan.strategy: Rollback is by PR revert. The migration shim from R8 (decision-7) writes contracts with `schemaVersion: 1.1` once a slice-aware orchestrator touches them; the reverted orchestrator running on a 1.1 contract must either translate back or refuse to load. The simplest safe revert path is to cap rollback to pipelines that haven't yet entered slice-aware orchestration — pipelines mid-implement on the slice-aware version cannot be rolled back without manual contract surgery.
steps: 1. Revert the PR via GitHub UI (creates revert commit on main).
2. Identify all pipelines with `schemaVersion: 1.1` contracts: `find .egg-state/contracts -name '*.json' | xargs grep -l 'schemaVersion.*1.1'`.

3. For pipelines NOT yet in implement phase: contract is forward-compatible because plan-phase only added a `slices[]` field; the reverted orchestrator reads from `phases[]` (still populated by the migration shim's two-way write — see R8 mitigation modification: shim must write BOTH `phases[]` and `slices[]` to support rollback). For pipelines IN implement phase under slice-aware orchestration: manual surgery — collapse `slices[]` back to a single `phases[]` entry covering all completed slice work, OR cancel the pipeline and re-run.
4. Branches `egg/issue-N/slice-M` left orphaned on origin: cleanup script: `git branch -r | grep '/slice-' | xargs git push origin --delete` (operator-confirmed).
5. Stacked PRs: close all child PRs (decision-2 says siblings continue, so this is potentially many PRs); the operator manually retargets any salvageable work onto a fresh `egg/issue-N` branch.
6. Orchestrator container rebuild picks up reverted code automatically.
7. Audit-log the entire rollback so the failure trace is reconstructable post-mortem.
rollback_plan.data_loss_risk: MEDIUM — partially-completed slice work is lost if rollback happens mid-implement. The migration shim's two-way write (writing both phases[] and slices[]) is the primary mitigation; without it, data loss is HIGH.
rollback_plan.downtime_risk: LOW for plan/refine-phase pipelines (forward-compatible). MEDIUM for implement-phase pipelines (manual surgery required).
rollback_plan.rollback_recommendation: Modify the R8 migration shim to write BOTH `phases[]` AND `slices[]` for one release cycle. This makes contracts dual-shape during the transition and enables clean rollback. Drop the `phases[]` write in the next minor release once #2137 is stable.

implementation_recommendations.recommendation: Land #2134 and #2139 dependencies BEFORE #2137; verify on origin/main before opening #2137's first PR.
implementation_recommendations.rationale: Issue text marks them hard prereqs. #2152 (reviewer_code fan-out tearout, part of #2139's cluster) is already merged per refine feedback Q5; verify #2134 (audit events for plan→contract) is also merged.

implementation_recommendations.recommendation: Introduce a typed `PipelineRef(pipeline_id, slice_id?)` value object at the message-bus boundary and refactor BRC lookups to take it (R1).
implementation_recommendations.rationale: Eliminates the silent mis-routing class. String-prefix conventions (`issue-N/slice-M`) are fragile because every consumer might parse them differently; types force the classification at compile/import time.

implementation_recommendations.recommendation: Forest validator is a pure function called from EVERY contract-load path, not just plan ingestion (R3). Property-test with hypothesis on randomly-generated DAGs.
implementation_recommendations.rationale: Defense in depth catches the silent-corruption class at runtime even if a future code path bypasses the ingestion validator.

implementation_recommendations.recommendation: Ship `max_parallel_slices = 5` as the default operational cap despite refine-phase decision-5 picking 'unbounded'. Make the architectural design support unbounded; the cap is a runtime config (R4).
implementation_recommendations.rationale: 120-container fan-out (15 slices × 8 roles) on first dogfooding will saturate gateway/Anthropic rate limits. Default cap of 5 lets operators raise empirically. Architecture remains capable of unbounded if the operator opts in.

implementation_recommendations.recommendation: Migration shim writes BOTH `phases[]` and `slices[]` for one release cycle to enable rollback (R8 + rollback plan).
implementation_recommendations.rationale: Without this, mid-implement rollback loses partial slice work. Two-way write costs ~5 lines of code and makes the rollback path safe.

implementation_recommendations.recommendation: Reconciler uses `git rebase --onto` for all stacked-PR rebases and detects parent-PR state (merged-via-UI / squash / closed / force-pushed) before acting (R2).
implementation_recommendations.rationale: Squash-merge is the most common GitHub merge mode; plain `git rebase` produces artificial conflicts. `git rebase --onto` is the documented fix in GitHub's own stacked-PR guidance.

implementation_recommendations.recommendation: Single-slice fast-path: len(slices) == 1 routes to today's monolithic flow with branch `egg/issue-N` (no slice suffix) and flat pipeline_id (R14).
implementation_recommendations.rationale: Most tickets are small. Slice overhead must amortize to zero on the common case. PR URL backward compatibility is a bonus.

implementation_recommendations.recommendation: Define internal slice-control APIs (`restart_slice`, `get_slice_status`, `list_slices`) as Python functions in the orchestrator, even though MCP wiring is deferred to #2199 (R11).
implementation_recommendations.rationale: Refine feedback Q4 explicitly requires this. Without it, #2199 becomes a much larger refactor.

implementation_recommendations.recommendation: Audit-log per-slice cycle consumption AND per-slice token spend so operators can size `max_parallel_slices` and `max_cycles` empirically (R4 + R7).
implementation_recommendations.rationale: Both caps were set by refine-phase HITL without load data. Empirical tuning post-rollout is the only way to validate them.

implementation_recommendations.recommendation: Document the per-slice security-lens limitation (R9) and the cost-inversion trade-off (R4) prominently in docs/guides/sdlc-pipeline.md before merging.
implementation_recommendations.rationale: These are deliberate trade-offs, not bugs. Operator-facing documentation prevents 'why did this happen' tickets.

performance_assessment.expected_quality_win: Large tickets (>33K LOC / >41 files per #2105 threshold) complete without compaction. Acceptance criterion: 'a previously-oversized ticket completes without compaction and is delivered as a stack of PRs.'
performance_assessment.cost_shape_change: INVERTED. Today's compacted run on a large ticket = cost C. New uncompacted run on the same ticket = cost roughly Nx where N is the slice count (3-7 typical, 10-15 worst-case from feedback Q1). For an 8-slice ticket, cost rises from ~1x to ~8x. Quality wins; cost doesn't.
performance_assessment.concurrency_envelope: Worst case 15 slices × 8 roles = 120 simultaneous agent containers. Default `max_parallel_slices = 5` (REC4) caps simultaneous work to ~40 containers — closer to today's gateway/Anthropic envelope.
performance_assessment.small-ticket impact: ZERO if REC7 single-slice fast-path is implemented. Without it, small tickets pay 5-10% slice-scheduling overhead.
performance_assessment.build_time_impact: Negligible — code changes are orchestrator/gateway/plan_parser; no Dockerfile changes.
performance_assessment.runtime_impact: Per-slice container startup adds ~2-5s to small tickets if the fast-path isn't taken; offset by parallelism win on large tickets.

security_assessment.threat_model: Cross-slice contamination of the BRC consensus protocol; cross-slice push to wrong branch via gateway misconfiguration; security regressions spanning two slices invisible to per-slice reviewer_security.
current_controls: Per-role / per-pipeline file-boundary allowlist in gateway/agent_restrictions.py
BRC tracker keyed on pipeline_id with reviewer authentication via mcp__brc__*
Reviewer_security and reviewer_concurrency lens reviewers (advisory today, CRITICAL after #1997)
proposed_controls: Slice-aware push authorization: gateway resolves (pipeline_id, slice_id, role) → expected branch pattern (R5)
Typed PipelineRef at the message-bus boundary preventing string-prefix mis-routing (R1, REC2)
Forest validator at every contract-load path catching multi-parent / cyclic shapes (R3, REC3)
Documented limitation that per-slice lens reviewers don't catch cross-slice regressions (R9)
Audit log extended with (pipeline_id, slice_id) tuple on every push and BRC message
security_assessment.residual_risk: MEDIUM — cross-slice security regressions remain invisible until #1997 promotes lenses to CRITICAL and a cross-slice pass is added (R9). Rest of the security surface is mechanical extension of existing controls and tractable.

compatibility_assessment.breaking_changes: Schema rename `contract.phases[]` → `contract.slices[]` is breaking for direct contract-JSON consumers; mitigated by R8 migration shim with two-way write for one release cycle (REC5).
compatibility_assessment.backward_compatibility: MEDIUM — pre-#2137 contracts loaded by post-#2137 orchestrator translate cleanly via the shim. Mid-implement rollback requires manual surgery without the two-way-write modification.
compatibility_assessment.forward_compatibility: GOOD — schemaVersion bump from 1.0 to 1.1 marks slice-aware contracts; future rev can drop the shim cleanly.
affected_systems: Gateway push authorization and PR creation
Plan parser and plan-phase prompt template
MCP tool surface (mcp__brc__*, mcp__sdlc__*, mcp__phase__*, mcp__task__*)
carve_outs: babysit_pr (#2063) — out of scope per refine decision-8; orthogonality preserved by REC15 typed PipelineMode
Per-slice MCP control (#2199) — exposed as internal API only per refine feedback Q4 + R11
Cross-slice lens-reviewer pass — deferred until #1997 promotes lenses to CRITICAL

github_stacked_prs_native_support.status: Now first-class in GitHub (private preview as of early 2026); see github.github.com/gh-stack/
github_stacked_prs_native_support.relevance: Decision-16's hybrid approach (auto-retarget + reconciler) aligns with GitHub's own model. Auto-retarget fires when parent merges via UI / `gh pr merge`; force-push or branch deletion breaks the chain.
edge_cases: Squash-merge: original commits disappear; plain `git rebase` produces artificial conflicts; `git rebase --onto` is the documented fix.
Mid-stack PR closure blocks all descendants; HITL escalation needed.
Cascading rebase conflicts can require manual resolution on every PR above the conflict point.
Linear history is required for merge; non-linear stacks need `gh stack rebase` or the Rebase Stack button.

anthropic_rate_limits.relevance: Decision-5 selected unbounded slice concurrency; Anthropic rate limits at higher concurrency tiers will throttle 100+ simultaneous agent containers. Refine feedback Q4 acknowledges this is not a current concrete blocker but `max_parallel_slices = 5` default (REC4) is conservative.
anthropic_rate_limits.mitigation: Operator-tunable cap; per-slice token-spend audit log for empirical sizing.

gha_queue_depth.relevance: Each slice may trigger GHA workflows on its branch; large stacks trigger many simultaneous GHA jobs. Today's repo runs comfortably; 10x fan-out has not been load-tested.
gha_queue_depth.mitigation: Operator-tunable `max_parallel_slices` cap; documentation of expected GHA queue impact.
